subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]
passage: Looking back, it's funny how fast it happened. Akash needed a shirt for his cousin's engagement, so we went into the mall store together. The first thing he picked up was a leather jacket: eleven thousand rupees. He laughed and put it back. Right beside it hung a cotton shirt for two thousand four hundred. "Aparna, look, this one's cheap," he said, already heading to the trial room. This is Akash, whose monthly pocket money is four thousand. I didn't say anything then. I just noticed that if we had come in through the other door, past the three-hundred-rupee T-shirts, the same shirt would have looked like a crime. Later, over chai, I told him. He went quiet, then laughed. "Two thousand four hundred is not cheap, na?"

qa.q: How much was the leather jacket?
qa.a: Eleven thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Akash call the shirt "cheap"?
qa.a: He had just seen the eleven-thousand-rupee jacket, so the shirt beside it seemed small, even though it was more than half his monthly pocket money.

qa.q: What choice did Aparna make, and why was the timing wise?
qa.a: Aparna stayed quiet in the shop and raised it over chai, which let Akash laugh and see it for himself instead of feeling judged at the counter.

qa.q: How might the shirt have looked to Akash if they had come in past the three-hundred-rupee T-shirts?
qa.a: Next to cheap T-shirts, the same shirt would have seemed expensive, and he might never have headed to the trial room.

grounding: A shopper notices a friend call a costly shirt cheap right after seeing a pricier jacket, showing how judgment follows the last thing seen.

subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]
passage:
Outing note, Saturday — Leela, residence supervisor
Took five first-years to the market street for festival shopping. Chetan wanted a kurta. At the first shop he tried on a silk sherwani priced at nine thousand, laughed and hung it back. The shopkeeper then showed a cotton kurta for two thousand. "That's so cheap after the sherwani," Chetan said, reaching for his wallet. On the bus he had told me his budget was one thousand. I asked him quietly, "If you'd seen this kurta first, what would you think of the price?" He paused. "Expensive, actually." He put the wallet away and bought an eight-hundred-rupee kurta two shops down. Next outing I'll suggest students write their budget on a slip before we start.

qa.q: What was Chetan's budget?
qa.a: One thousand.

qa.q: Why did the two-thousand-rupee kurta seem cheap to Chetan?
qa.a: He had just tried on a nine-thousand-rupee sherwani, so the kurta looked small beside it, even though it was double his budget.

qa.q: Which question did Leela ask, and why did it work?
qa.a: "If you'd seen this kurta first, what would you think of the price?" It made Chetan judge the price on its own instead of against the sherwani.

qa.q: How might the order of showing clothes look from the shopkeeper's side?
qa.a: For the shopkeeper, showing the costly sherwani first makes the next item look like a bargain and helps sales; Chetan was reacting to that order.

grounding: A young supervisor watches a student feel a kurta is cheap right after trying a costly sherwani, and helps him judge it on its own.

passage:
Sunday
Went bag shopping with Ritu. At the first store, she picked up a designer handbag, eighteen thousand, gasped and put it down like it was hot. Then the salesman showed her a "simple one" for four thousand five hundred. "After that, this is nothing!" she said. Ritu, who was complaining on Friday that she can't pay her phone bill. I wanted to say something but didn't know how without sounding like her mother. So I said, "Let's see the stalls outside first, then decide." Outside, bags were five hundred. She looked at the photo of the four-thousand-five-hundred bag on her phone, then at the stall, and said, "Oh. It's actually expensive, isn't it?" She bought a seven-hundred one. Felt like a good friend today.
Kalyani

qa.q: How much was the designer handbag?
qa.a: Eighteen thousand.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani hesitate to say something in the store?
qa.a: Kalyani didn't know how to raise it without sounding like Ritu's mother, and worried about seeming preachy.

qa.q: What choice did Kalyani make, and why did it help?
qa.a: Suggesting they see the stalls outside first; five-hundred-rupee bags gave Ritu a new comparison, so she saw the price clearly herself. 👍

qa.q: How might the four-thousand-five-hundred bag have looked to Ritu if she had seen the stalls first?
qa.a: She would probably have seen it as expensive from the start, especially with the phone bill on her mind, instead of "nothing" beside the designer bag.

grounding: A young adult watches a friend feel a costly bag is cheap after seeing a designer one, and helps her find a truer comparison.

subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]
passage: At the crowded cloth shop in Meerut's main bazaar, Sachin, nineteen, needed something for his sister's wedding. His cousin Kashish had come along to keep him within budget: fifteen hundred rupees. The shopkeeper, smiling, first pulled out a velvet blazer with gold buttons. 'Fifteen thousand, sir. Pure quality.' Sachin laughed and shook his head. Then the man showed a printed silk shirt. 'Only three thousand.' 'Only three!' Sachin said. 'After that blazer this is almost free.' Kashish watched him reach for his wallet. Last week he had said a two-thousand shirt was 'robbery'. 'Sachin, what did you say about the two-thousand one?' He paused, hand on the wallet. 'That was different.' 'Different how? This one's more.' He looked at the blazer, then the shirt. 'Oh,' he said slowly. Kashish noticed he put his wallet back in his pocket, but his eyes kept going to the silk.

qa.q: How much was Sachin's budget for the shirt?
qa.a: His budget was fifteen hundred rupees.

qa.q: Why did Sachin say the silk shirt was 'almost free'?
qa.a: He had just seen the fifteen-thousand blazer, so three thousand felt tiny by comparison, even though it was double his budget.

qa.q: What did Kashish's question make Sachin notice, and what did he choose?
qa.a: Kashish reminded him he'd called a two-thousand shirt robbery, so he saw the price only looked cheap after the blazer and put his wallet back.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper see the blazer he showed first?
qa.a: The shopkeeper probably shows it on purpose, knowing it makes the next item look like a bargain to most customers.

grounding: A cousin watches a young man call a costly shirt cheap after being shown a very expensive blazer, and helps him notice that the comparison shaped the judgment.
